## Introduction 

The following document outlines a partial reanalysis of data on CpG methylation status in human skeletal muscle in response to resistance exercise training, followed by detraining and subsequent retraining [@seaborne2018;@seaborne2018b]. Most of the relevant code is explicitly shown here, whereas the version of this case study included in the manuscript has been stripped of some details.


## Raw data and pre-processing

```{r}
#| label: dependencies
#| eval: true

library(GEOquery)      # For accessing the raw data
library(minfi)         # For pre-processing of raw data
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(stringr)
library(maxprobes)     # For filtering cross-reactive probes 
library(seqwrap)


# Load color scale 
source(here::here("analysis/figures/figure-opts.R"))


```


Raw data are downloaded from the [Gene Expression Omnibus](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/) using the accession number [GSE114763](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE114763). 


```{r}
#| label: paths
#| eval: true

# Prepare data download. 
# Note for use in the present repo: 
# raw_data and derived data are gitignored so safe for 
# large files. If code-re-use, check the download folder before committing 
# changes to git. 

# The GEO ID
gse_id   <- "GSE114763"

# Set download directories
raw_dir  <- here::here("analysis/data/raw_data", gse_id)
idat_dir <- file.path(raw_dir, "idat")
der_dir  <- here::here("analysis/data/derived_data")

dir.create(idat_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create(der_dir,  recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

```

### Downloading data

Sample titles and characteristics are read from the SOFT text view of the series, which returns the metadata of all 40 samples. The supplementary archive (`GSE114763_RAW.tar`, ~722 MB) provides the IDAT files.

```{r}
#| label: download
#| eval: true


# The metadata (pheno_raw) and the raw data IDAT files are cached after 
# downloading once. 

# A function for retrying connection to GEO for downloading large data.
# This was created after issues with downloading the large zipped archive
# from GEO. 
retry_url <- function(expr, tries = 5, pause = 5) {
  call <- substitute(expr)          # re-evaluated on each attempt
  env  <- parent.frame()
  for (i in seq_len(tries)) {
    out <- try(eval(call, env), silent = TRUE)
    if (!inherits(out, "try-error")) return(out)
    if (i < tries) Sys.sleep(pause * i)
  }
  stop("failed after ", tries, " attempts: ",
       conditionMessage(attr(out, "condition")))
}

# Series-level metadata
#
# The metadata contains file names and titles include 
# time-points and participant information. 
pheno_file <- file.path(raw_dir, "pheno_raw.rds")

if (!file.exists(pheno_file)) {
  soft_url <- paste0("https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi",
                     "?acc=", gse_id, "&targ=gsm&form=text&view=brief")

  soft <- retry_url({
    res <- curl::curl_fetch_memory(soft_url)
    if (res$status_code != 200) stop("HTTP ", res$status_code)
    strsplit(rawToChar(res$content), "\r?\n")[[1]]
  })

  # one record per sample; "!Sample_<key> = <value>" lines within each
  kv <- tibble::tibble(record = cumsum(startsWith(soft, "^SAMPLE")),
                       line   = soft) |>
    dplyr::filter(startsWith(line, "!")) |>
    tidyr::separate(line, into = c("key", "value"), sep = " = ",
                    extra = "merge") |>
    dplyr::mutate(key = stringr::str_remove(key, "^!Sample_"))

  # characteristics are themselves "<key>: <value>" pairs
  characteristics <- kv |>
    dplyr::filter(key == "characteristics_ch1") |>
    tidyr::separate(value, into = c("key", "value"), sep = ": ",
                    extra = "merge") |>
    dplyr::filter(key %in% c("gender", "age", "weight", "height")) 

  # Cleaning the metadata for downstream processing. 
  pheno_raw <- kv |>
    dplyr::filter(key %in% c("geo_accession", "title")) |>
    dplyr::bind_rows(characteristics) |>
    tidyr::pivot_wider(id_cols = record, names_from = key,
                       values_from = value) |>
    dplyr::select(-record) |> 

        mutate(title_sep = title) |> 
        separate(title_sep, into = c("seq_sample_id", "timeid"), sep = ":") |>
        mutate(timeid = gsub(" Muscle_", "", timeid)) |> 
        mutate(timeid = gsub("Participant_", "", timeid)) |> 
        mutate(timeid = gsub("7wk_", "7wk", timeid)) |> 
        
         separate(timeid, into = c("time", "participant", "replicate"), sep = "_") |> 
      # Making time-point more obvious
        mutate(time = case_when(
              time == "Baseline" ~ "1_baseline", 
              time == "Acute" ~ "2_acute", 
              time == "7wkLoading" ~ "3_loading", 
              time == "7wkUnloading"  ~ "4_unloading", 
              time == "7wkRe-oading" ~ "5_reloading"
        )) |> 
        # Fixing meta-data details
        mutate(weight = gsub(" kg", "", weight), 
               height = gsub("cm", "", height), 
               weight = as.numeric(weight), 
               height = as.numeric(height), 
               age = as.numeric(age)) |> 
        # Fix a misprinted participant id
        mutate(participant = gsub("P006", "006", participant)) 
  

  saveRDS(pheno_raw, pheno_file)
}

pheno_raw <- readRDS(pheno_file)

# Double check 40 expected samples
stopifnot(nrow(pheno_raw) == 40)

# Download and extract raw IDAT files.
# IDATs are distributed gzipped; minfi reads decompressed files
tar_file <- file.path(raw_dir, paste0(gse_id, "_RAW.tar"))

if (!file.exists(tar_file)) {
  # ~722 MB; increase the timeout for slow connections
  options(timeout = 60 * 60)
  retry_url(GEOquery::getGEOSuppFiles(gse_id, baseDir = dirname(raw_dir),
                                      makeDirectory = TRUE))
}

if (length(list.files(idat_dir, pattern = "\\.idat$")) == 0) {
  utils::untar(tar_file, exdir = idat_dir)

  # Unzip idat files
  gz <- list.files(idat_dir, pattern = "\\.idat\\.gz$", full.names = TRUE)
  invisible(lapply(gz, R.utils::gunzip, overwrite = TRUE, remove = TRUE))
}

```

### Metadata summary

A total of 40 samples were downloaded from the Gene Expression Omnibus ([GSE114763](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE114763)). The identified metadata (@tbl-meta-samples) corresponds to the metadata published in [@seaborne2018b] (see table 2 in @seaborne2018b).

Seaborne et al. removed two samples after preliminary analysis, (samples `SkM_Epi_Mem_1` and `SkM_Epi_Mem_39`), we will do the same.


```{r}
#| label: tbl-meta-samples
#| tbl-cap: "Sample metadata retreived from GEO ([GSE114763](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE114763)) corresponding to @seaborne2018b".
#| echo: false


library(gt)

pheno_raw |> 
      summarise(.by = participant, 
                weight = mean(weight), 
                height = mean(height), 
                age = mean(age)) |> 
      mutate(participant = gsub("00", "", participant)) |> 
      select(participant, age, height, weight) |> 
      gt() |> 
      cols_label(participant = "Participant", 
                 age = "Age (years)", 
                 weight = "Weight (kg)", 
                 height = "Height (cm)")
      
      
```


## Case study description

```{r}
#| label: case-description
#| echo: false

# Double check gender 
# pheno_raw |> 
#      distinct(gender)
# Confirm all males


# Get sample metadata into text
sample_metadata <- pheno_raw |> 
      
      summarise(.by = participant, 
                weight = mean(weight), 
                height = mean(height), 
                age = mean(age)) |> 
      pivot_longer(weight:age) |> 
      summarise(.by = name, 
                m = mean(value), 
                s = sd(value)) |> 
      mutate(unit = c("kg", "cm", "years")) |> 
      mutate(stat = paste0(sprintf("%.1f", round(m, 1)), 
                           " (", 
                           sprintf("%.1f", round(s, 1)), 
                           ") ", 
                           unit)) 

age <- filter(sample_metadata, name == "age") |> pull(stat)
height <- filter(sample_metadata, name == "height") |> pull(stat)
weight <- filter(sample_metadata, name == "weight") |> pull(stat)

```


> Seaborne et al. [@seaborne2018;@seaborne2018b] investigated whether human skeletal muscle retains an epigenetic memory of earlier hypertrophy-inducing resistance training. For this aim, previously untrained male participants (age, [mean (SD)] `r age`; weight, `r weight`; height, `r height`) completed a sequential design with two seven-week periods of resistance-exercise training (RET) intersected with a 7-week unloading period without RET. RET periods included two weekly sessions targeting lower limbs (seven exercises) and one weekly session targeting the upper body (5 exercises; 4 sets of 10 repetitions per exercise). Skeletal muscle biopsies were sampled from m. vastus lateralis on five occasions: before the intervention, 30 min after the first exercise session, and after the completion of each of the 7-week periods. Genomic DNA was extracted from muscle biopsy samples (DNeasy Kit, Qiagen, Manchester, UK) and bisulfite converted before amplification, fragmentation, and hybridization using the Illumina Infinium Human MethylationEPIC Beadchip protocol [@seaborne2018;@seaborne2018b]. 


The Sentrix slide (chip) and array position are recovered from the IDAT file names (e.g. `GSM3149860_201496860025_R01C01_Grn.idat`) and retained as potential technical covariates in subsequent analyses. `Basename` is the file stem that `minfi` uses to locate the red/green channel pair.

The samples are distributed as described in [@seaborne2018;@seaborne2018b] with one participant dropping out from the study prior to the last sampling time-point. One participant have duplicate arrays at one time-point. After removal of samples based on preliminary QC-analysis (see @seaborne2018b), the full data set contains 38 samples with no technical duplicates. 

```{r}
#| label: tbl-metadata-count
#| eval: true
#| tbl-cap: "Samples per time-point and participant."


idat_stems <- list.files(idat_dir, pattern = "_Grn\\.idat$") |>
  stringr::str_remove("_Grn\\.idat$")

array_info <- tibble::tibble(stem = idat_stems) |>
  tidyr::separate(stem, into = c("geo_accession", "slide", "array"),
                  sep = "_", remove = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::mutate(Basename = file.path(idat_dir, stem))

metadata <- pheno_raw |>
      # Removing outlier sample, see "Quality Control of DNA Methylation Probes"
      # in @seaborne2018b
      filter(!grepl("SkM_Epi_Mem_1:", title), 
             !grepl("SkM_Epi_Mem_39:", title)) |> 
      
  tibble::as_tibble() |>
  dplyr::select(geo_accession,
                title,
                participant,
                gender,
                age, 
                time) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    label = stringr::str_remove(title, "^SkM_Epi_Mem_\\d+:\\s*")) |>
  dplyr::left_join(array_info, by = "geo_accession")

stopifnot(!anyNA(metadata$time), !anyNA(metadata$participant))

# 38 arrays: 8 participants x 5 time points with missing values for on 
# participant.

metadata |> 
      summarise(.by = c(time, participant), 
                n = n()) |> 
      pivot_wider(names_from = time, values_from = n) |> 
      select(Participant = participant, 
             Baseline = `1_baseline`, 
             Acute = `2_acute`, 
             Loading = `3_loading`, 
             Unloading = `4_unloading`, 
             Reloading = `5_reloading`) |> 
      gt() |> 
      tab_spanner(label = "Sample time-points", columns = "Baseline":"Reloading")
      



```

### Reading IDAT and array-level quality control

We will use the `minfi` package [@fortin2014] to read the raw data and perform quality control, filtering and normalization. As a first step, array-level filtering is done using detection p-values where methylated and unmethylated positions are compared to negative control positions. This comparison produces a p-value used to identify problematic genomic positions. As shown below (@fig-array-qc), array-level aggregates show mean values < 0.01.    


```{r}
#| label: fig-array-qc
#| fig-cap: "Array-level quality control. Mean detection p-values and fraction of failed genomic positions per array subdivided by time-point."
#| eval: true

rgset <- minfi::read.metharray(metadata$Basename, extended = TRUE, force = TRUE)

# Check that orders correspond
stopifnot(identical(colnames(rgset), basename(metadata$Basename)))

colnames(rgset) <- metadata$geo_accession


det_p <- minfi::detectionP(rgset)

# 
qc <- tibble::tibble(
  geo_accession = colnames(det_p),
  mean_det_p    = colMeans(det_p),
  frac_failed   = colMeans(det_p > 0.01))

qc |> 
      inner_join(pheno_raw |> 
                       select(geo_accession, time)) |> 
      ggplot(aes(mean_det_p, frac_failed, color = time)) + 
      geom_point() +
      labs(x = "Array-level mean detection p-value", 
           y = "Fraction of failed genomic positions (p > 0.01)", 
           color = "Time-point")
```



```{r}

# Below is the suggested workflow for confirming sex. We expect only males and 
# the function indficate that only one sex is present which should suffice as 
# confirmation.
# predicted   <- minfi::getSex(minfi::mapToGenome(msetraw))
# qc$pred_sex <- predicted$predictedSex

# All samples pass quality control
keep_samples <- qc$geo_accession[qc$mean_det_p < 0.01]
# length(keep_samples)

rgset    <- rgset[, keep_samples]
det_p    <- det_p[, keep_samples]
metadata <- metadata |> dplyr::filter(geo_accession %in% keep_samples)
```

### Normalization and probe filtering

Functional normalization [@fortin2014] is used because the study design can be expected to result in global methylation differences. Functional normalization removes technical variation captured by the array control probes without assuming a common methylation distribution across samples [@fortin2014]. Probes are then removed if they (1) fail detection in any retained sample, (2) overlap common SNPs at the target CpG or single-base extension site, (3) appear on published lists of cross-reactive EPIC probes (using the [`maxprobes`](https://github.com/markgene/maxprobes/) package), or (iv) map to the sex chromosomes (all male cohort).

```{r}
#| label: normalise-filter
#| eval: true



# Functional normalization
gset <- minfi::preprocessFunnorm(rgset, ratioConvert = FALSE)

# Initial number of probes
nprobes_init <- dim(gset)[1]

## (i) detection
det_p  <- det_p[match(minfi::featureNames(gset), rownames(det_p)), ]
keep   <- rowSums(det_p < 0.01) == ncol(gset)
gset   <- gset[keep, ]

# Number of probes after filtering
nprobes_detectionfilter <- dim(gset)[1]

## (ii) SNP-affected probes 
gset <- minfi::dropLociWithSnps(gset, snps = c("SBE", "CpG"), maf = 0)

nprobes_snp <- dim(gset)[1]

## (iii) cross-reactive probes 
gset <- maxprobes::dropXreactiveLoci(gset)

nprobes_cross <- dim(gset)[1]

## (iv) sex chromosomes 
anno <- minfi::getAnnotation(gset)
gset <- gset[!anno$chr %in% c("chrX", "chrY"), ]

nprobes_final <- dim(gset)[1]


## Clean up memory 
rm(rgset); gc()



```

`r nprobes_init` normalized probes were filtered based on detection which retained `r nprobes_detectionfilter`, after SNP-overlap (n = `r nprobes_snp`), cross-reactivity (n = `r nprobes_cross`) and sex-chromosome mapping filtering, n = `r nprobes_final` remained in the data set. 

### Calculation of methylation quantities

An Illumina array detecting methylation values produces arbitrary signals for the unmethylated (U) and methylated (M) portion of the i^th^ genomic position. Converting these two values to a methylation score is done trough the calculation of a &beta; value.

$$
\beta_i = \frac{M_i}{M_i+U_i + c}
$$
The bias constant c, is added to the denominator to avoid large variations in the &beta; score when probe intensities are low [@bibikova2006]. This value was set to $c = 100$ to achieve regularization of the &beta; values in cases where both M and U were small [@bibikova2006], which is also the default in the `minfi` package when `type = "illumina"`. However, the successful choice of c is noted to depend on the pre-processing of the data (see `?minfi::getBeta`). 

Inspecting the normalized signals representing methylated and unmethylated probes indicate that the constant will only have a minor impact on most sites as both *M* and *U* are >> 100 @fig-raw-data-characteristics A.   

```{r}
#| label: fig-raw-data-characteristics
#| fig-cap: "Methylated and Unmethylated signals accross samples and a subset of the genomic sites (n = 1000) shows that most signals are well above 100 (A). Calculation of beta; values with different selections of *c* indicate minor differences in the overall distribution of values (B). Both figures have the relative density on the y axis (not shown)"

# Extract the methylated and unmethylated signals
M <- minfi::getMeth(gset)
U <- minfi::getUnmeth(gset)

# Set the number of probes
n <- 1000

# Figure A: Methylated and Unmethylated signals accross samples. 
set.seed(1)

# Sample sites 
sites <- sample(rownames(M), n)

figa <- data.frame(M)[sites,] |> 

   
      tibble::rownames_to_column(var = "id") |> 
      
      pivot_longer(starts_with("GSM"), values_to = "M") |> 
      
      inner_join(
            data.frame(U)[sites,] |> 
                  tibble::rownames_to_column(var = "id") |> 
                  pivot_longer(starts_with("GSM"), values_to = "U")     
      ) |> 
      pivot_longer(cols = M:U, 
                   names_to = "signal") |> 
      ggplot(aes(value, group = paste0(signal,name), 
                 color = signal)) + 
      geom_line(stat = "density") +
      scale_x_log10()  + 
      theme_classic() + 
      theme(axis.title.y = element_blank(), 
            axis.ticks.y = element_blank(), 
            axis.line.y = element_blank(), 
            axis.text.y = element_blank()) + 
      scale_color_manual(values = colors) + 
      labs(x = "Normalized signal (AU)", 
           color = "Signal type")


figb <- data.frame(M)[sites,] |> 
 
   
      tibble::rownames_to_column(var = "id") |> 
      
      pivot_longer(starts_with("GSM"), values_to = "M") |> 
      
      inner_join(
            data.frame(U)[sites,] |> 

                  tibble::rownames_to_column(var = "id") |> 
                  pivot_longer(starts_with("GSM"), values_to = "U")     
      ) |> 
      
     mutate(beta0 = M / (M + U + 0), 
            beta50 = M / (M + U + 50),
            beta100 = M / (M + U + 100)) |> 
      dplyr::select(id, name, beta0:beta100) |>

      pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("beta"), 
                   names_to = "constant", 
                   values_to = "beta") |> 
      mutate(constant = as.numeric(gsub("beta", "", constant))) |> 
      
      ggplot(aes(beta, group = constant, color = as.factor(constant))) +
      geom_line(stat = "density") +
       theme_classic() + 
      theme(axis.title.y = element_blank(), 
            axis.ticks.y = element_blank(), 
            axis.line.y = element_blank(), 
            axis.text.y = element_blank(), 
            axis.title.x = ggtext::element_markdown()) + 
      scale_color_manual(values = colors) + 
      labs(x = "&beta;-values", 
           color = "Offset constant")
      

cowplot::plot_grid(figa, figb, ncol = 1)

```

We decide to go for the default value of *c* = 100 for the calculation of the &beta; values. 
&beta;-values are restricted to the 0 to 1 space, and although this is an intuitive metric for understanding the methylation status at a specific genomic site (e.g., as a percentage methylation), it is an inconvenient quantity for a statistical model that expects normally distributed errors [@laird2010; @du2010]. Indeed, when applying a Gaussian model to identify differentially methylated genomic sites, a logit transformation of the &beta;-values results in more favorable diagnostics [@du2010]. The logit transformation of the &beta; values results in M-values. 

$$
M = \log_2 \left( \frac{\beta}{1-\beta} \right)
$$

The logit transformation (using a base 2 logarithm) puts the methylation values on a scale with no upper or lower bounds (-ininf;, &ininf;, @fig-beta-mval). This transformation is done on the &beta;-values directly to avoid missing c in the calculation.  


```{r}
#| label: fig-beta-mval
#| fig-cap: "The logit transform of &beta; values gives M-values."
#| echo: false


beta <- seq(from = 0.001, to = 0.999, by = 0.001)
Mval <- log2(beta/(1-beta))

data.frame(Mval, beta) |> 
      ggplot(aes(Mval, beta)) + geom_line() + 
      theme_classic() + 
      labs(x = "M-values", y = "&beta;-values") + 
      theme(axis.title.y = ggtext::element_markdown())

```

### Inferential error rates across models 

Next, we will compare the models using type I error rate, power and discrimination determined from permutation of within-participant relabeled data. This relabeling establishes a null distribution for statistical tests performed using the *within-participant design*. The design keeps the within-participant correlation. Our approach is similar to what was described in [@gadbury2008].

We will perform the experiment on permuted data from a subset of genomic sites distributed across different strata of &beta; values. 

A fixed number of sites is sampled from each &beta;-value stratum. Within every permutation, a random subset of those sites receives a *known* effect (adding a known average effect) while the remainder are left untouched. Sites without an effect estimate the *type I error rate*, sites with an effect estimate *power*.

We will use the *M-value scale* to add the effect to permuted data with effect assignment *redrawn in every permutation*. The &beta;-values are derived from the manipulated M-values. A shift of &delta; M units is exactly the fixed-effect parameter of the Gaussian model and proportionally to &delta;&times;log(2) for the linear-predictor shift of the &beta; model with the logit link. This means that no model is favored by the parameterization. Our approach differs here from @gadbury2008. We fix the effect sizes while @gadbury2008 uses empirical effect sizes from the data. Our simplified approach enables comparisons between model fitting procedures at known effect sizes and signs across strata of &beta; values.

In the code chunk below, a single site is used to show the workflow. &beta; values are calculated from the `gset` object and transformed to M values. We are using the first row of the M value matrix and join the values with the meta data. Within each participant, time is re-sampled to create a permuted time factor. Using the permuted time factor, an average effect (&delta; = 0.3) is added to all observations belonging to the permuted time-point `3_loading`. Data are back-transformed to the &beta; scale and both model types are fitted.

We will use a set of different inferential alternatives to establish the most appropriate model and test for our data set. In small samples, linear mixed model parameter p-values from the Wald test are anti-conservative [@luke2017]. When the restricted maximum likelihood (REML) is used in place of maximum likelihood and small sample size-corrections are used (Kenward-Roger or Satterthwaite approximations of degrees of freedom) the type I error rates are controlled at the nominal level [@luke2017]. However, for the generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) with link functions, such as beta regression, the restricted maximum likelihood is not clearly defined [@maestrini2024]. When comparing different REML implementations, @maestrini2024 found that GLMM fitted with REML leads to a reduction in small sample bias and that the use of REML probably should be more widely adopted. The choice of algorithm can be made based on software availability [@maestrini2024]. REML is implemented also for GLMM in the glmmTMB package with the option `REML=TRUE`. For Gaussian models, the results from `glmmTMB` replicates the results of `lme4::lmer`. However, the documentation also says that performance of REML in non-Gaussian models should be verified by simulations (see `?glmmTMB::glmmTMB`).

In addition to REML for mitigation of small sample bias, the Satterthwaite correction is widely adopted in Gaussian mixed-effects models to approximate the denominator degrees of freedom for t-tests of parameter estimates [@kuznetsova2017]. Similarly to REML estimation for GLMM's, the Satterthwaite approximation is indicated for use "at your own risk" (see `?glmmTMB::dof_satt`).


```{r}

# Illustrating data preparation and model settings for a set of 
# candidate models for the methylation data set.

# Prepare data 
beta_vals <- getBeta(gset, offset = 100)
m_vals <- log2(beta_vals / (1 - beta_vals))

# Setting the seed for site selection and time permutation
set.seed(1)

# Selecting a random site for testing
y <- data.frame(y = m_vals[sample(1:nrow(m_vals), 1),]) |> 
      tibble::rownames_to_column(var = "geo_accession" ) 

# Organizing the data into aformat suitable for single model 
# fit. 
dat <- metadata |> 
      select(geo_accession, participant, time) |> 
      inner_join(y) |>
      # Permutation of time within participant
      group_by(participant) |> 
      mutate(time_permute = sample(time, replace = FALSE)) |> 
      ungroup() |> 
      mutate(msim = if_else(time_permute == "3_loading", 
             y + 0.3, y), 
             betasim = plogis(msim * log(2))) 


# A general purpose summary function for ML/REML fits
temp_summary_fun <- function(m) {
      
      is_reml <- m$modelInfo$REML
      # LRT p-value
      if(!is_reml) {
            lrt_mod <- drop1(m, test = "Chisq")
            lrt_p <- lrt_mod["time_permute", "Pr(>Chi)"]
            
      } else { lrt_p <- NA }
      # Wald p-value (restricted to paremeter 3_loading)
      wald_p <- coef(summary(m))$cond["time_permute3_loading", "Pr(>|z|)"]
      # Wald p-value Satterthwaite
      wald_p_satter <- coef(summary(m, ddf = "satterthwaite"))$cond["time_permute3_loading", "Pr(>|t|)"]
      
      data.frame(lrt_p = lrt_p, 
                 wald_p = wald_p, 
                 wald_p_satter = wald_p_satter)
      
}
```

The estimated effects (`r round(es_mmod,2)` and `r round(es_betamod,2)`) for the model on M-values and &beta; values respectively are comparable but will differ due to compression in the &beta; values model.

For the single site used in the illustration above, p-values differs between models (M- vs &beta;-values), estimator (ML vs. REML), and usage of the Satterthwaite's approximation of the degrees of freedom @tbl-model-comp-illustration). The will be the basis of evaluation of the models in the permutation experiment. 

In the permutation experiment, the added fixed effect sizes are multiplied by 1 or -1 in a balanced fashion to create the direction of the effect. At an extreme site (&beta;-values close to 0 or 1), adding or subtracting &delta; will either compress towards the boundary or move estimates towards 0.5. Since these scenarios are not equally detectable and the two models disagree about the variance function in extreme regions, we can evaluate the effect of selecting one model over the other also for the mean estimate.

The source code for the permutation experiment can be run in full using the script `analysis/R/methylation-error-permutation.R`. Below we check if files are available from a previous run, if not the script runs and stores data in `analysis/data/derived_data/permutation/`. 



```{r}

if (length(perm_files) == 0) source(
      here::here("analysis/R/methylation-error-permutation.R")
      )

n_perm <- length(perm_files)
```

### Loading permutation study results

A total of `r n_perm` sets of permutations where performed with 1000 sites in each set over 5 &beta; value strata. @tbl-permutation-evals shows the number of failed models among all model fits for the four fitted model specifications. 

```{r}
#| label: reading-permutation-data
#| eval: true
#| label: tbl-permutation-evals

### Reading the results back
spike_time <- "3_loading"

perm_files <- list.files(out_dir, pattern = "^perm_\\d+\\.RDS$", full.names = TRUE)
perm       <- lapply(perm_files, readRDS)

perm_summaries <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(perm, `[[`, "summaries"))
perm_designs   <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(perm, `[[`, "design"))
perm_evals     <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(perm, `[[`, "evaluations"))



# Which coefficients with the simulated effect.
#
# The added effect shifts only the samples labelled `spike_time` under the 
# permuted labels. `spike_time` is set to 3_loading and
# 1_baseline is the reference level.

# alt_terms also accepts and omnibus test (not used here)
# Instead, the omnibus test is saved per target in the eval slot.
alt_terms <- c(paste0("time_permute", spike_time))

# Attach the per-iteration effects (delta, sign, stratum) to every test.
# is_alt is ground truth for a (site, term) pair, not for a site.
perm_dat <- perm_summaries |>
      dplyr::inner_join(perm_designs,
                        by = c("iter", "target" = "id")) |>
      # Carry the per-fit convergence code across from the evaluation slot so
      # that failed fits can be dropped from the Wald error rates too. This
      # matters because the arms can fail at different rates, which would
      # quietly change which sites each arm is scored on.
      dplyr::inner_join(perm_evals |>
                              dplyr::select(iter, target, model, convergence),
                        by = c("iter", "target", "model")) |>
      # delta is signed, so the test must be != 0 -- `delta > 0` would classify
      # every downward-spiked site as a null and contaminate the reference.
      dplyr::mutate(is_alt = delta != 0 & term %in% alt_terms)

stopifnot(any(perm_dat$is_alt))

# Convergence failures are dropped silently by seqwrap_summarise (NULL entries
# are removed before rbind), so differential failure between the models would
# quietly change what is being compared.

# Sort out number of failed p-values (Wald statistics)
pvals_wald <- perm_summaries |> 
      summarise(.by = model, 
                n_coefs_wald = n(), 
                failed_p = sum(is.na(p_wald)), 
                failed_satt = sum(is.na(p_satt)))

# Sort out number of p-values (LR test)
pvals_lrt <- perm_evals |> 
      summarise(.by = model, 
                n_models_lrt = n(), 
                failed_lrt = sum(is.na(pval))) |> 
      mutate(failed_lrt = if_else(grepl("_reml", model), NA, failed_lrt)) 



perm_evals |>
      dplyr::summarise(.by = c(model),
                       n_fits     = dplyr::n(),
                       n_fail     = sum(convergence != 0),
                       prop_fail  = mean(convergence != 0)) |> 
      inner_join(pvals_wald) |> 
      inner_join(pvals_lrt) |> 
      
      mutate(estimator = if_else(grepl("_reml", model), "REML", "ML"), 
             model = gsub("_reml", "", model), 
             model = if_else(model == "beta", "&beta;", "M")) |> 
      dplyr::select(model, estimator, n_fits, n_fail, n_coefs_wald, failed_p, 
                    failed_satt, n_models_lrt, failed_lrt) |> 
      gt() |> 
      gt::cols_label(model = "Model", 
                     estimator = "Estimator", 
                     n_fits = "Number of fits", 
                     n_fail = "Failed fits", 
                     n_coefs_wald = md("Number of <br>parameter values"), 
                     failed_p = md("Number of failed <br>Wald p-values"), 
                     failed_satt = md("Number of <br>failed Satterthwaite p-values"), 
                     n_models_lrt = md("Number of models<br>evaluated for LRT"), 
                     failed_lrt = "Failed LRT p-values") |> 
      fmt_markdown(columns = "model")
      
```

### Determining the type I error rate

The type I error rates are estimated from sites and parameter estimates without added effects. The unaffected parameters on a site with an added effect are nominally null, but could affect the the full model. However, preliminary inspection of this effect did not raise concerns. Therefore, all null-parameters are used in the estimating the type I error rate.

### Determining the power

When evaluating the empirical power we must take the type I error rate into account as a higher type I error rate also spills over into increased power [@lloyd2005]. As the type 1 error rates differs between inferential procedures (@fig-permutation-type1), we will compare power the same size [@lloyd2005]. From each p-value procedure among the null effects a critical value is calculated as $\hat{c}$ which is the &alpha;-quantile of the null distribution of p-values. Power is then determined as the proportion of true non-null effects with $p \le \hat{c}$. We will use only the contrast used for the added effect (`time_permute3_loading`) to build the null distribution of p-values and we set the &alpha; level to 0.05. 

The actual size varies between the &beta;-value strata (proportion of type I errors in @fig-permutation-type1), so the calibration can be made at two levels. A single critical value per cell answers what happens when a procedure is run at one threshold calibrated to 5% overall, which is the realistic situation. A critical value per cell and stratum answers which procedure detects more *at equal size within a stratum*, and is the comparison that is not confounded by the stratum-wise differences in calibration. Both are computed below; the stratum-resolved figure uses the second.

```{r}
#| label: power-setup
#| eval: true

# The nominal level.
alpha <- 0.05

# Monte Carlo critical value.
#
# The functions first sorts the p-values and then 
# sets then uses the alpha * length(p) as the critical value.
crit_value <- function(p, alpha) {
      p <- sort(p[!is.na(p)])
      k <- floor(alpha * length(p))
      # Too few draws to place a rejection region at this level: reject nothing.
      if (k < 1) return(0)
      p[k]
}

# One row per (model, test type, iteration, site). We use the wald-type 
# contrasts and the data from the LRT test (ML only).
#
# `is_alt` is ground truth. These are the sites with added effect. 
power_dat <- dplyr::bind_rows(

      perm_dat |>
            dplyr::filter(convergence == 0, term %in% alt_terms) |>
            dplyr::select(model, iter, target, betacat, delta, delta_abs,
                          estimate, p_wald, p_satt) |>
            tidyr::pivot_longer(cols = c(p_wald, p_satt),
                                names_to = "type",
                                values_to = "pval"),

      perm_evals |>
            dplyr::filter(convergence == 0) |>
            # The REML arms carry no LRT (see eval_fun in the permutation
            # script), and arrive here as NA rather than as absent rows.
            dplyr::filter(!is.na(pval)) |>
            dplyr::inner_join(perm_designs,
                              by = c("iter", "target" = "id")) |>
            dplyr::mutate(type = "LRT", estimate = NA_real_) |>
            dplyr::select(model, iter, target, betacat, delta, delta_abs,
                          estimate, type, pval)) |>

      # Applied to nulls and alternatives together: dropping the Satterthwaite
      # failures from one side only would change which sites a cell is scored
      # on. The retained counts are reported per cell in @tbl-power-calibration.
      dplyr::filter(!is.na(pval)) |>
      dplyr::mutate(is_alt = delta != 0,
                    sgn = sign(delta),
                    model = factor(model),
                    type = factor(type, levels = c("p_wald", "p_satt", "LRT")))

stopifnot(any(power_dat$is_alt), any(!power_dat$is_alt))

```

```{r}
#| label: power-critical-values
#| eval: true

# Calibration, pooled over strata.
crit_global <- power_dat |>
      dplyr::filter(!is_alt) |>
      dplyr::summarise(.by = c(model, type),
                       n_null = dplyr::n(),
                       # Actual size at the nominal cut-off.
                       size_nominal = mean(pval <= alpha),
                       c_hat = crit_value(pval, alpha),
                       # By construction this should sit at alpha. It is kept
                       # as a check on the rejection region, not as a result.
                       size_adjusted = mean(pval <= c_hat))

# Calibration within stratum.
crit_strata <- power_dat |>
      dplyr::filter(!is_alt) |>
      dplyr::summarise(.by = c(model, type, betacat),
                       n_null = dplyr::n(),
                       size_nominal = mean(pval <= alpha),
                       c_hat = crit_value(pval, alpha),
                       size_adjusted = mean(pval <= c_hat))

# The rejection region must be conservative in every cell.
stopifnot(all(crit_global$size_adjusted <= alpha + 1e-6),
          all(crit_strata$size_adjusted <= alpha + 1e-6))

```

Power is estimated per iteration and then averaged over iterations with the permutation as the resampling unit. The Monte Carlo (permutation iteration) standard error is taken across the `r n_perm` iterations. The effect grid is balanced by construction (five sites per &delta; &times; sign cell within every stratum), but convergence failures can unbalance it, so pooled figures are averages of cell means rather than raw proportions.

```{r}
#| label: power-estimation
#| eval: true

# Per-iteration power in the finest cell of the design: model, test type,
# stratum, effect magnitude and direction. Three calibrations are carried side
# by side so that the effect of the adjustment is readable.
power_cell <- power_dat |>
      dplyr::filter(is_alt) |>
      dplyr::inner_join(crit_global |> dplyr::select(model, type,
                                                     c_global = c_hat),
                        by = c("model", "type")) |>
      dplyr::inner_join(crit_strata |> dplyr::select(model, type, betacat,
                                                     c_stratum = c_hat),
                        by = c("model", "type", "betacat")) |>
      dplyr::summarise(.by = c(model, type, betacat, delta_abs, sgn, iter),
                       n_sites = dplyr::n(),
                       pow_nominal = mean(pval <= alpha),
                       pow_adj_global = mean(pval <= c_global),
                       pow_adj_stratum = mean(pval <= c_stratum))

# Aggregate power_cell to a requested grouping. The mean is taken over the
# finer cells within an iteration first, so that an unbalanced cell (caused by
# a convergence failure) does not weight the pooled estimate.
power_agg <- function(dat, by = character()) {

      dat |>
            dplyr::summarise(
                  .by = dplyr::all_of(c("model", "type", "iter", by)),
                  dplyr::across(dplyr::starts_with("pow_"), mean)) |>
            tidyr::pivot_longer(cols = dplyr::starts_with("pow_"),
                                names_to = "calibration",
                                values_to = "power") |>
            dplyr::summarise(
                  .by = dplyr::all_of(c("model", "type", "calibration", by)),
                  m.power = mean(power),
                  s.power = stats::sd(power),
                  n_iter = dplyr::n(),
                  mcse = s.power / sqrt(n_iter)) |>
            dplyr::mutate(lo = m.power - 1.96 * mcse,
                          hi = m.power + 1.96 * mcse)
}

power_overall  <- power_agg(power_cell)
power_delta    <- power_agg(power_cell, by = c("delta_abs"))
power_strata   <- power_agg(power_cell, by = c("betacat", "delta_abs"))
power_sign     <- power_agg(power_cell, by = c("betacat", "delta_abs", "sgn"))

```

```{r}
#| label: power-labels
#| eval: true

# Labels shared by the table and the figures below, matching those used for
# the type I error rate.
lab_model <- function(x) {
      dplyr::recode(as.character(x),
                    beta      = "&beta;<sub>ML</sub>",
                    beta_reml = "&beta;<sub>REML</sub>",
                    m         = "M<sub>ML</sub>",
                    m_reml    = "M<sub>REML</sub>")
}

lab_type <- function(x) {
      factor(dplyr::recode(as.character(x),
                           p_wald = "Wald p-values",
                           p_satt = "Satterthwaite DDF",
                           LRT    = "Omnibus LRT"),
             levels = c("Wald p-values", "Satterthwaite DDF", "Omnibus LRT"))
}

lab_betacat <- function(x) {
      factor(dplyr::case_when(x == "xlow"  ~ "0 - 0.2",
                              x == "low"   ~ "0.2 - 0.4",
                              x == "mid"   ~ "0.4 - 0.6",
                              x == "high"  ~ "0.6 - 0.8",
                              x == "xhigh" ~ "0.8 - 1"),
             levels = c("0 - 0.2", "0.2 - 0.4", "0.4 - 0.6",
                        "0.6 - 0.8", "0.8 - 1"))
}

lab_sign <- function(x) {
      factor(dplyr::if_else(x > 0, "&delta; > 0", "&delta; < 0"),
             levels = c("&delta; > 0", "&delta; < 0"))
}

# The effect magnitudes actually present, used as axis breaks.
deltas <- sort(unique(power_cell$delta_abs))
```

@tbl-power-calibration shows the critical value ($\hat{c}$) of every inferential procedure, aggregated over &beta; categories, together with power before and after the adjustment. Power depends on the effect magnitude and is shown in the figure below (@fig-permutation-power).

The two directions of the added effect are in theory not equally detectable at the extremes of the &beta;-value distribution. At a site with a &beta; value close to 0 or 1, an effect that moves the mean towards the boundary is compressed, whereas an effect of the same magnitude on the M scale that moves the mean towards 0.5 is not. Only small differences were seen between models across &beta; strata (@fig-permutation-power)  

A rejection in the wrong direction is not a detection. Since the sign of the added effect is known, the proportion of rejections (p < 0.05) whose estimate carries the opposite sign can be determined directly. The estimate of the &beta; model is on the logit scale, which preserves the sign, so the two model types are comparable. @tbl-power-sign-discordance summarizes the discordant effects across the the REML models with the Satterthwaite DDF correction. The model type do not to any meaningful degree differ in the sign error. When effects are larger, discordant effects are expected to a lesser degree [@gelman2014].

```{r}
#| label: tbl-power-sign-discordance
#| eval: true

# Sign-discordant rejections (type S, @gelman2014) among the size-adjusted
# rejections. The omnibus LRT is excluded: it has no signed estimate.
#
# Rates are formed from POOLED counts rather than as the mean of per-iteration
# rates. A cell with no rejections in a given permutation has no rate to
# average, so averaging silently drops that permutation and weights the result
# towards the permutations that rejected most.
sign_rejections <- power_dat |>
      dplyr::filter(is_alt, type != "LRT") |>

      dplyr::filter(pval < 0.05) |>
      dplyr::mutate(discordant = sign(estimate) != sgn)

# Full-resolution breakdown, kept for inspection. Note that the cells of this
# table are thin: at the resolution of model x test x stratum x effect x sign
# the discordant counts are single digits, which is why nothing below is
# reported at that resolution.
sign_discordance <- sign_rejections |>
      dplyr::summarise(.by = c(model, type, betacat, delta_abs, sgn),
                       n_rejected = dplyr::n(),
                       n_discordant = sum(discordant),
                       prop_discordant = n_discordant / n_rejected)



# (i) The resolved result: type S risk against the magnitude of the effect,
# for each model arm. The Satterthwaite cell is used throughout, matching the
# threshold that the power figures are built on.
sign_rejections |>
      dplyr::filter(type == "p_satt") |>
      dplyr::summarise(.by = c(model, delta),
                       n_rejected = dplyr::n(),
                       n_discordant = sum(discordant),
                       prop_discordant = n_discordant / n_rejected) |> 
      filter(model %in% c("beta_reml", "m_reml")) |> 
      pivot_wider(names_from = model, 
                  values_from = c(n_rejected, n_discordant, prop_discordant)) |> 
      arrange(delta) |> 
      dplyr::select(delta, 
                    n_rejected_beta_reml, n_discordant_beta_reml, prop_discordant_beta_reml, 
                    n_rejected_m_reml, n_discordant_m_reml, prop_discordant_m_reml) |> 
      gt()  |> 
      tab_spanner(label = md("&beta;<sub>REML</sub>"), 
                  columns = c(n_rejected_beta_reml, n_discordant_beta_reml, prop_discordant_beta_reml)) |> 
      tab_spanner(label = md("M<sub>REML</sub>"), 
                  columns = c(n_rejected_m_reml, n_discordant_m_reml, prop_discordant_m_reml)) |> 
           fmt_number(columns = c(prop_discordant_beta_reml, 
                                  prop_discordant_m_reml), 
                      decimals = 4) |> 
      cols_label(delta = md("&delta;"), 
                 n_rejected_beta_reml = "N rejected",
                 n_discordant_beta_reml = "N discordant", 
                 prop_discordant_beta_reml = md("Proportion<br>discordant"), 
                    n_rejected_m_reml = "N rejected", 
                 n_discordant_m_reml = "N discordant", 
                 prop_discordant_m_reml= md("Proportion<br>discordant")) |> 
      fmt_number()
      
```


The power analysis indicates that the inferential procedures do not differ in the effects that they detect once size is accounted for. What is left to separate them is the machinery of the test itself: the standard error that the fit reports and the reference distribution that the standard error is judged against. A rejection at the nominal level occurs when $|\hat\delta| > c \times \widehat{\text{SE}}$, with $c = 1.96$ for the Wald test and $c = t_{0.975, \nu}$ for the Satterthwaite test at the approximated denominator degrees of freedom &nu;. The estimate is very nearly common to the four procedures: the two tests within an arm are two readings of one fit and share it exactly, the M arm is unchanged by the switch from ML to REML, which cannot move the fixed effects of a Gaussian mixed model, and the two &beta; arms agree to within `r sprintf("%.3f", reml_shift$beta_vs_beta_reml)` M units at the worst site of the whole experiment. The product $c \times \widehat{\text{SE}}$ — the half-width of the rejection region — is then very nearly the *only* quantity in which they can differ, and it is the quantity that has to account for the differences in type I error rate seen in @fig-permutation-type1.

```{r}
#| label: se-setup
#| eval: true

# Standard errors on a common scale, on the true nulls only. The null cells
# are the ones the type I error rates are read from, and the standard error
# is a property of the fit rather than of the reference distribution, so a
# single value per (arm, iteration, site) carries both tests.
#
# The beta arm reports on the logit scale, where a shift of delta M units is
# a shift of delta*log(2); dividing by log(2) puts both arms in M units. This
# is the same conversion used in @tbl-model-comp-illustration and in the bias
# section below.
# The two tests within an arm are two readings of one fit, so they share the
# estimate exactly. Across estimators the agreement has to be checked rather
# than assumed: REML cannot change the fixed effects of a Gaussian mixed model
# at all, but it can change them for the beta GLMM, whose restricted
# likelihood is not the same object. Both are checked together, since
# agreement on the Gaussian side is what shows that the arms are being read
# correctly.
reml_shift <- perm_dat |>
      dplyr::filter(convergence == 0, term %in% alt_terms) |>
      dplyr::select(model, iter, target, estimate) |>
      tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = estimate) |>
      dplyr::summarise(
            m_vs_m_reml       = max(abs(m - m_reml), na.rm = TRUE),
            beta_vs_beta_reml = max(abs(beta - beta_reml), na.rm = TRUE))

stopifnot(reml_shift$m_vs_m_reml < 1e-3)

se_dat <- perm_dat |>
      dplyr::filter(convergence == 0, term %in% alt_terms, delta == 0) |>
      dplyr::mutate(
            divisor = dplyr::if_else(grepl("^beta", model), log(2), 1),
            se_M    = std.error / divisor,
            # Satterthwaite can return a degenerate denominator degrees of
            # freedom on a fit whose participant variance sits on the zero
            # boundary (@fig-re-sd-failedsatterthwaite). The inner replacement
            # keeps qt() off those values rather than letting it warn.
            ddf_ok  = !is.na(ddf) & ddf > 0,
            # The multiplier that each test applies to the standard error.
            p_wald  = stats::qnorm(0.975),
            p_satt  = dplyr::if_else(
                  ddf_ok,
                  stats::qt(0.975, dplyr::if_else(ddf_ok, ddf, 1)),
                  NA_real_)) |>
      dplyr::select(model, iter, target, betacat, se_M, ddf, p_wald, p_satt) |>
      tidyr::pivot_longer(cols = c(p_wald, p_satt),
                          names_to = "type",
                          values_to = "crit") |>
      dplyr::mutate(type = factor(type, levels = c("p_wald", "p_satt")),
                    # The half-width of the rejection region in M units.
                    halfwidth = crit * se_M)

# The permutation is the resampling unit, as it is everywhere else: a site
# level summary is formed within an iteration first and the iterations are
# then averaged. The within-iteration summary is a median because the
# standard error of the beta arm is right skewed in the extreme strata, where
# a few sites with near-boundary fitted means dominate a mean.
se_stratum <- se_dat |>
      dplyr::filter(type == "p_wald") |>
      dplyr::summarise(.by = c(model, betacat, iter),
                       med_se = stats::median(se_M, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
      dplyr::summarise(.by = c(model, betacat),
                       m.se = mean(med_se),
                       mcse = stats::sd(med_se) / sqrt(dplyr::n()))

# The four arms are fitted to the same site in the same iteration, so the
# half-widths can be compared within a site rather than between marginal
# distributions. Everything is expressed relative to the M model fitted by
# REML and tested against the Satterthwaite reference, i.e. the procedure
# that held the nominal level in @fig-permutation-type1.
hw_ref <- se_dat |>
      dplyr::filter(model == "m_reml", type == "p_satt") |>
      dplyr::select(iter, target, betacat, hw_ref = halfwidth)

hw_ratio <- se_dat |>
      dplyr::inner_join(hw_ref, by = c("iter", "target", "betacat")) |>
      dplyr::filter(!is.na(halfwidth), !is.na(hw_ref)) |>
      dplyr::mutate(ratio = halfwidth / hw_ref) |>
      dplyr::summarise(.by = c(model, type, betacat, iter),
                       med_ratio = stats::median(ratio, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
      dplyr::summarise(.by = c(model, type, betacat),
                       m.ratio = mean(med_ratio),
                       mcse = stats::sd(med_ratio) / sqrt(dplyr::n()))

# The Satterthwaite multiplier on its own: how much of the widening in panel B
# is bought by the reference distribution rather than by the estimator.
satt_mult <- se_dat |>
      dplyr::filter(type == "p_satt", !is.na(crit)) |>
      dplyr::summarise(.by = c(model, betacat, iter),
                       med_crit = stats::median(crit),
                       med_ddf  = stats::median(ddf, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
      dplyr::summarise(.by = c(model, betacat),
                       m.crit = mean(med_crit),
                       m.ddf  = mean(med_ddf))

# The two steps, as percentages, for the text. The estimator step is the REML
# standard error against its ML counterpart within a stratum; the reference
# step is the Satterthwaite multiplier against the normal quantile it
# replaces. Both are summarised across strata as a range, since neither turns
# out to depend on the stratum.
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f", 100 * (x - 1))

se_step <- se_stratum |>
      dplyr::mutate(estimator = dplyr::if_else(grepl("_reml", model),
                                               "reml", "ml"),
                    family = dplyr::if_else(grepl("^beta", model),
                                            "beta", "m")) |>
      dplyr::select(family, estimator, betacat, m.se) |>
      tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = estimator, values_from = m.se) |>
      dplyr::mutate(ratio = reml / ml)

crit_step <- satt_mult |>
      dplyr::filter(grepl("_reml", model)) |>
      dplyr::mutate(ratio = m.crit / stats::qnorm(0.975))

```

```{r}
#| label: fig-permutation-se
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "Standard errors and rejection regions across &beta;-value strata under the null. (A) Median standard error of the spiked contrast in M-value units. (B) Half-width of the rejection region, c &times; SE, for each test, formed per site and expressed relative to the M<sub>REML</sub> model tested against the Satterthwaite reference (dashed line at 100%). Points are means over permutations of the within-permutation median, error bars are &plusmn;1.96 Monte Carlo standard errors."

figA <- se_stratum |>
      dplyr::mutate(model = lab_model(model),
                    betacat = lab_betacat(betacat)) |>

      ggplot(aes(model, m.se)) +
      geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = m.se - 1.96 * mcse,
                        ymax = m.se + 1.96 * mcse),
                    width = 0.5) +
      geom_point(size = 3, shape = 21, fill = "white") +
      ggh4x::facet_wrap2(~ betacat, ncol = 5, strip = strip) +
      theme_classic() +
      theme(axis.title.x = ggtext::element_markdown(),
            axis.text.x = ggtext::element_markdown(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
            axis.title.y = ggtext::element_markdown()) +
      labs(x = NULL,
           y = "Standard error<br>(M-value units)")

figB <- hw_ratio |>
      dplyr::mutate(model = lab_model(model),
                    betacat = lab_betacat(betacat),
                    type = lab_type(type)) |>

      ggplot(aes(model, 100 * m.ratio, shape = type, fill = type)) +
      geom_hline(yintercept = 100, lty = 2, colour = "gray") +
      geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = 100 * (m.ratio - 1.96 * mcse),
                        ymax = 100 * (m.ratio + 1.96 * mcse)),
                    width = 0.5,
                    position = position_dodge(width = 0.3)) +
      geom_point(size = 3, position = position_dodge(width = 0.3)) +
      ggh4x::facet_wrap2(~ betacat, ncol = 5, strip = strip) +
      theme_classic() +
      theme(axis.title.x = ggtext::element_markdown(),
            axis.text.x = ggtext::element_markdown(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
            axis.title.y = ggtext::element_markdown(),
            legend.position = "bottom",
            legend.title = element_blank()) +
      scale_shape_manual(values = c(21, 24)) +
      scale_fill_manual(values = colors) +
      labs(x = "Model",
           y = "Rejection region half-width<br>(% of M<sub>REML</sub>, Satterthwaite DDF)")

fig_se <- cowplot::plot_grid(figA, figB,
                             ncol = 1,
                             rel_heights = c(1, 1.2),
                             labels = c("A", "B"))

fig_se

```

@fig-permutation-se separates the two mechanisms. Panel A shows that the standard error depends on the estimator rather than on the model type: the ML fits report a smaller standard error than their REML counterparts in every stratum, by `r pct(min(se_step$ratio))` to `r pct(max(se_step$ratio))`%, which is the expected consequence of estimating the variance components without accounting for the estimation of the fixed effects. The stratum, by contrast, moves both arms together, and the &beta; and M arms differ from each other by little. Panel B combines that standard error with the multiplier the test applies to it. A Wald test on an ML fit gives the narrowest rejection region of the four procedures and therefore rejects most often; replacing ML by REML widens it by the amount above, and replacing the normal quantile by the Satterthwaite one adds a further `r pct(min(crit_step$ratio))` to `r pct(max(crit_step$ratio))`% at a median of about `r sprintf('%.0f', mean(crit_step$m.ddf))` denominator degrees of freedom. The two steps are close to independent of the &beta; stratum and of the model type, and together they take the ML Wald procedure to the one that held the nominal level in @fig-permutation-type1.

This is the whole of the difference between the procedures. The estimates are all but shared, the size-adjusted power is shared, and what remains is a rejection region that four procedures draw at four slightly different widths. The type I error rates of @fig-permutation-type1 are the direct consequence: a procedure that draws its rejection region a few percent too narrow rejects a few percent too often under the null, and buys nothing for it under the alternative.







### Exaggeration of the reported effect

The sections above concern what the procedures *decide*. This one concerns what gets *reported* once a decision has been made. A site is declared differentially methylated only when its estimate is large enough to clear the threshold, so the estimates that are reported are a selected subset of the estimates that were made, and their average magnitude exceeds the effect that generated them. This is the type M error of @gelman2014, the companion of the sign error in @tbl-power-sign-discordance, and it is a property of thresholded reporting rather than of either model.

No comparison of the two models against the added effect is attempted here, because this experiment cannot support one. The effect is added to the observed M values, $m' = m + \delta x$, and $x$ is exactly the column of the design matrix that the contrast is read from. The variance components of the Gaussian arm are estimated from residual contrasts orthogonal to that column space and are therefore identical for $m$ and $m'$, which makes the fixed effect satisfy $\hat\delta(m + \delta x) = \hat\delta(m) + \delta$ as an algebraic identity rather than as an estimate — it returns the added effect exactly, on any data, for any &delta;. The &beta; arm has no such identity, since its response, $\text{plogis}(m'\log 2)$, is a nonlinear transform of the spiked values rather than a shift of them. Any difference between the arms measured against &delta; is that asymmetry and not a property of the estimators, so the exaggeration below is read within an arm rather than between them.

The two arms still have to be put on a common scale to appear in the same figure. Because $\text{logit}(\beta) = M \times \log(2)$, a shift of &delta; M units is a shift of $\delta \log(2)$ in the linear predictor of the &beta; model, so dividing the &beta;-model estimate by $\log(2)$ puts both arms in M units. This is the same conversion used for the single site in @tbl-model-comp-illustration. Only the REML arms are carried forward, since the estimate and not the test is what is at issue.

```{r}
#| label: bias-type-m
#| eval: true

# One row per (arm, iteration, site) on the spiked contrast, both arms in M
# units. The estimates do not depend on the reference distribution, so this
# works from perm_dat directly rather than from the pivoted power_dat.
est_dat <- perm_dat |>
      dplyr::filter(convergence == 0, term %in% alt_terms,
                    model %in% c("beta_reml", "m_reml")) |>
      dplyr::mutate(est_M = dplyr::if_else(grepl("^beta", model),
                                           estimate / log(2), estimate))

# Exaggeration ratio: the mean magnitude of the estimates that survive the
# size-adjusted threshold, relative to the effect that generated them. The
# Satterthwaite cell is used, and the threshold is the one calibrated within
# stratum, so this is conditioned on exactly the rejections counted in
# @fig-permutation-power.
crit_satt <- crit_strata |>
      dplyr::filter(type == "p_satt") |>
      dplyr::mutate(model = as.character(model)) |>
      dplyr::select(model, betacat, c_stratum = c_hat)

# The permutation is the resampling unit, as it is everywhere else: the ratio
# is formed within a permutation and the permutations are then averaged. The
# same 1,000 sites are reused in every iteration and share a single
# relabelling within it, so the pooled number of rows would badly overstate
# the precision available.
type_m <- est_dat |>
      dplyr::filter(delta != 0, !is.na(p_satt)) |>
      dplyr::inner_join(crit_satt, by = c("model", "betacat")) |>
      dplyr::filter(p_satt <= c_stratum) |>
      dplyr::summarise(.by = c(model, delta_abs, iter),
                       n_rejected = dplyr::n(),
                       ratio = mean(abs(est_M)) / dplyr::first(delta_abs)) |>
      dplyr::summarise(.by = c(model, delta_abs),
                       m.ratio = mean(ratio),
                       mcse = stats::sd(ratio) / sqrt(dplyr::n()),
                       n_iter = dplyr::n()) |>
      dplyr::mutate(lo = m.ratio - 1.96 * mcse,
                    hi = m.ratio + 1.96 * mcse)

type_m_small <- type_m |>
      dplyr::filter(delta_abs == min(delta_abs)) |>
      dplyr::summarise(lo = min(m.ratio), hi = max(m.ratio))

type_m_large <- type_m |>
      dplyr::filter(delta_abs == max(delta_abs)) |>
      dplyr::summarise(lo = min(m.ratio), hi = max(m.ratio))

```

```{r}
#| label: fig-bias-type-m
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Exaggeration (type M) ratio: the mean magnitude of the estimates that survive the size-adjusted threshold, divided by the effect that generated them. A ratio of one, the dashed line, means that a reported estimate is on average the effect it came from. The ratio grows as the effect shrinks because a small effect is only detected on the permutations in which it was over-estimated. Error bars are 95% Monte Carlo intervals over permutations."

type_m |>
      dplyr::mutate(Model = lab_model(model)) |>

      ggplot(aes(delta_abs, m.ratio, colour = Model, shape = Model,
                 group = Model)) +
      geom_hline(yintercept = 1, lty = 2, colour = "gray60") +
      geom_line() +
      geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), width = 0.03) +
      geom_point(size = 2) +
      theme_classic() +
      theme(legend.position = "bottom",
            legend.title = element_blank(),
            legend.text = ggtext::element_markdown(),
            axis.title.x = ggtext::element_markdown()) +
      scale_colour_manual(values = colors) +
      scale_shape_manual(values = c(21, 24)) +
      scale_x_continuous(breaks = deltas) +
      labs(x = "Added effect (|&delta;|, M-value units)",
           y = "Exaggeration ratio")

```

The exaggeration ratio is largest for the smallest effects, reaching `r sprintf("%.2f", type_m_small$lo)`–`r sprintf("%.2f", type_m_small$hi)` at |&delta;| = `r min(deltas)` and falling to `r sprintf("%.2f", type_m_large$lo)`–`r sprintf("%.2f", type_m_large$hi)` at |&delta;| = `r max(deltas)` (@fig-bias-type-m). This is not a defect of either model, and the two arms behave alike. An effect of the smallest size is detected only on the permutations in which it happened to be over-estimated, so the estimates that pass the threshold are, on average, several times the effect that generated them; an effect large enough to be detected reliably is reported at close to its true magnitude. It is a reason to report effect sizes for all sites rather than only for the significant ones, and it applies whichever model is fitted.






## Full model run

```{r}

# The annotation file
gset <- readRDS(here::here("analysis/data/derived_data/seaborne-gset-normalized.RDS"))
anno <- minfi::getAnnotation(gset)
nsites <- nrow(anno)

```


The unfiltered Illumina EPIC data has over 800 000 CpG positions. After filtering the available dataset contained `r nsites` CpG positions. Since the strategy here is to detect differentially methylated positions (DMP) we will fit a model per available position using the &beta;- and M-values and their respective model (generalized linear model with &beta; and normal likelihoods, respectively). 

### Loading the full model results

The four arms are fitted by `analysis/R/methylation-case-full.R`, which writes one file per arm to `analysis/data/derived_data/full_v2/` together with a small timing sidecar. The arms are the same four as in the permutation study above, read with the same two Wald reference distributions per contrast; the omnibus LRT is not part of the full run.

```{r}
#| label: full-model-import
#| eval: true

# The results directory is VERSIONED in the same way as the permutation
# directory: full_v2/ holds the four-arm run (beta, beta_reml, m, m_reml)
# with `p_wald` and `p_satt` per contrast, the latter on the REML arms only.
# The earlier two-arm files in the derived_data root (beta-model-full.RDS,
# m-model-full.RDS) carry a different summary schema and are superseded by it.
full_dir   <- here::here("analysis/data/derived_data/full_v2")
full_arms  <- c("beta", "beta_reml", "m", "m_reml")
full_files <- file.path(full_dir, sprintf("%s.RDS", full_arms))

# Unlike the permutation study, a missing file is NOT refitted on the fly: the
# four arms together are close to a day of wall-clock time (see the timings
# reported below), so what is missing is reported instead.
if (!all(file.exists(full_files)))
      stop("missing arm files in full_v2/: ",
           paste(basename(full_files[!file.exists(full_files)]),
                 collapse = ", "),
           ". Run analysis/R/methylation-case-full.R first.",
           call. = FALSE)

# Optionally trim the read to a subset of fixed effects. All terms are kept by
# default; the four time contrasts plus the intercept over 770 441 sites is
# ~3.9 million rows per arm, so setting this to the contrast(s) actually
# reported is the lever if the render is memory-bound.
full_keep_terms <- NULL

# One arm at a time. Each arm object is on the order of 10^2 MB, so the
# per-fit diagnostics are joined on WITHIN the arm and the arm is dropped
# before the next one is read, rather than binding four whole arms and joining
# afterwards.
read_full_arm <- function(file) {

      arm <- readRDS(file)

      summaries <- if (is.null(full_keep_terms)) arm$summaries else
            dplyr::filter(arm$summaries, term %in% full_keep_terms)

      # Carry convergence, singularity and the participant SD across from the
      # evaluation slot, exactly as perm_dat does above: the arms fail at
      # different rates, so a failed fit has to be droppable from the tests
      # rather than quietly changing which sites each arm is scored on.
      dat <- summaries |>
            dplyr::inner_join(dplyr::select(arm$evaluations, target,
                                            convergence, singular, re_sd),
                              by = "target") |>
            # Constant within an arm, so stored as factors: at this number of
            # rows the same three labels as character vectors are hundreds of
            # MB of pointers for no extra information.
            dplyr::mutate(
                  model     = factor(arm$model, levels = full_arms),
                  estimator = factor(if (isTRUE(arm$meta$reml)) "REML" else "ML",
                                     levels = c("ML", "REML")),
                  scale     = factor(arm$meta$scale, levels = c("beta", "M")))

      # seqwrap_summarise() drops failed targets rather than returning empty
      # rows, so a target present in one slot and not the other would silently
      # shrink the arm here.
      stopifnot(nrow(dat) == nrow(summaries))

      evaluations <- dplyr::mutate(
            arm$evaluations,
            model = factor(arm$model, levels = full_arms))

      # `class` and `message` come back as character vectors named by target;
      # the names are dropped so the bound frame does not carry four sets of
      # them.
      errors <- if (NROW(arm$errors)) {
            arm$errors |>
                  dplyr::mutate(class   = unname(class),
                                message = unname(message),
                                model   = factor(arm$model, levels = full_arms))
      } else NULL

      out <- list(dat = dat, evaluations = evaluations,
                  errors = errors, meta = arm$meta)

      rm(arm, summaries)
      gc()

      out
}

full_list <- lapply(full_files, read_full_arm)

# full_dat:    one row per (model, site, fixed effect) -- the frame the
#              per-position analysis is read from.
# full_evals:  one row per (model, site) -- fit-level diagnostics.
# full_errors: one row per condition raised (warnings and errors), by stage.
# full_meta:   one row per arm -- what was fitted, on how many cores, how long.
full_dat    <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(full_list, `[[`, "dat"))
full_evals  <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(full_list, `[[`, "evaluations"))
full_errors <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(full_list, `[[`, "errors"))
full_meta   <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(full_list, `[[`, "meta"))

rm(full_list)
gc()

# `reml` in the evaluation slot is read off the fit object, not off the arm
# name (see eval_fun in the script), so this is the check that the arm
# labelling agrees with what was actually estimated. The arms are also all
# fitted on the same set of sites, which is what makes them comparable
# site-by-site.
stopifnot(
      setequal(as.character(full_evals$model), full_arms),
      all(full_evals$reml == grepl("_reml$", as.character(full_evals$model))),
      length(unique(full_meta$k)) == 1L,
      length(unique(full_meta$n)) == 1L)

# The number of sites and samples the full run was fitted on.
n_full_sites   <- unique(full_meta$k)
n_full_samples <- unique(full_meta$n)

# The contrasts: 1_baseline is the reference level, so the time terms are the
# differences from baseline. The intercept is present in full_dat but is not a
# contrast and is excluded here.
full_terms <- setdiff(unique(full_dat$term), "(Intercept)")

# The timing sidecar written by the same script, read separately so the
# per-arm cost is available without loading the arms.
full_timing <- readRDS(file.path(full_dir, "timing.RDS"))

```

The full run fitted `r n_full_sites` positions in `r n_full_samples` samples per arm, giving `r nrow(full_dat)` estimated parameters across the four arms and `r length(full_terms)` contrasts against baseline (`r paste(full_terms, collapse = ", ")`).
