### Computational time

The four arms were fitted one `seqwrap()` call at a time, and the elapsed time of each call is recorded in the timing sidecar written alongside the results (@tbl-timing-full). That says what this run cost. It does not say what the cost is a *function* of, which is the question anyone sizing a different design has to answer, and it cannot be read off a single number per arm.

`analysis/R/methylation-timing-experiment.R` answers it by timing the same four arms on sub-samples of the same data, varying one thing at a time: the number of targets ($k$), the model, and the number of arrays. Everything inside the timed region is what the full run did --- same data, same `arguments`, same `summary_fun` (the Satterthwaite denominator df is a real cost and is paid here too), same `eval_fun`, same `return_models = FALSE`, same core count --- so the fitted intercept and slope are in the units of the full run rather than in units of a benchmark. Cells are run in a randomised order, and a fixed anchor cell is re-run throughout to detect any drift in machine speed over the two hours the experiment takes.

```{r}
#| label: reading-timing
#| eval: true
#| echo: false

timing_dir <- here::here("analysis/data/derived_data/timing_v1")

timing_cells <- readRDS(file.path(timing_dir, "timing-cells.RDS"))
timing_scaling <- readRDS(file.path(timing_dir, "timing-scaling.RDS"))

# The core count is part of the measurement, not a footnote: the slope is the
# per-target cost at that width and the intercept is largely cluster start-up,
# which grows with the number of workers. It is read from the record rather
# than written into the prose.
timing_cores <- unique(timing_scaling$session$cores)

stopifnot(
      length(timing_cores) == 1L,
      identical(as.integer(timing_cores), as.integer(unique(full_timing$cores))))

# Size block: is the cost linear in k?
#
# `timing-scaling.RDS` carries an `exponent` and a `linear` flag from a log-log
# fit of elapsed time on k. That fit has NO intercept term, so it tests whether
# elapsed time is PROPORTIONAL to k, which cannot hold when there is a fixed
# per-call cost of about a minute: at the k used here the intercept dominates,
# and the exponent it returns (~0.16 to 0.35) measures that dominance rather
# than the scaling. The saved `linear` column is therefore FALSE for all four
# arms and is not read here.
#
# The test with the intercept restored is elapsed = a + b * k^c, with linearity
# at c = 1, and the curvature check is whether a quadratic term is needed. Both
# are computed from the raw cells.
timing_size <- dplyr::filter(timing_cells, block == "size")

timing_fit <- timing_size |>
      dplyr::group_by(arm) |>
      dplyr::group_modify(function(d, key) {
            lin <- stats::lm(elapsed ~ k, data = d)
            quad <- stats::lm(elapsed ~ k + I(k^2), data = d)

            nl <- tryCatch(
                  stats::nls(
                        elapsed ~ a + b * k^c,
                        data = d,
                        start = list(a = stats::coef(lin)[[1]],
                                     b = stats::coef(lin)[[2]],
                                     c = 1),
                        control = stats::nls.control(maxiter = 200,
                                                     warnOnly = TRUE)),
                  error = function(e) NULL)

            # Profile intervals on an nls fit can fail to converge; the Wald
            # interval is the fallback, and NA is reported rather than a number
            # of unknown provenance if both fail.
            ci <- if (is.null(nl)) c(NA_real_, NA_real_) else {
                  s <- summary(nl)$coefficients["c", ]
                  prof <- tryCatch(suppressMessages(stats::confint(nl, "c")),
                                   error = function(e) NULL,
                                   warning = function(w) NULL)
                  if (is.null(prof)) {
                        s[["Estimate"]] + c(-1.96, 1.96) * s[["Std. Error"]]
                  } else {
                        as.numeric(prof)
                  }
            }

            data.frame(
                  r2 = summary(lin)$r.squared,
                  exponent = if (is.null(nl)) NA_real_ else stats::coef(nl)[["c"]],
                  exponent_lo = ci[1],
                  exponent_hi = ci[2],
                  p_quadratic = summary(quad)$coefficients["I(k^2)", 4])
      }) |>
      dplyr::ungroup()

# The scaling and extrapolation tables, joined on the arm and put in the
# labelling used everywhere else in this document.
timing_tab <- timing_scaling$scaling |>
      dplyr::select(arm, scale, estimator, overhead_s, per_target_s) |>
      dplyr::inner_join(timing_fit, by = "arm") |>
      dplyr::inner_join(
            dplyr::select(timing_scaling$extrapolation,
                          arm, k_full, predicted_h, observed_h, error_pct),
            by = "arm") |>
      dplyr::mutate(per_target_ms = per_target_s * 1000)

# The largest k the experiment ever fitted, against the k the prediction is
# made at: the extrapolation factor is the thing being asked to hold.
timing_k_max <- max(timing_size$k)
timing_extrap_factor <- unique(timing_tab$k_full) / timing_k_max

# Marginal cost in the two blocks that hold k fixed.
#
# `per_target_ms` in those blocks is elapsed / k, so it still carries the
# per-call overhead amortised over k targets -- at k = 2000 that is about 31 ms
# of the ~45 ms reported, and it is the same 31 ms in every row, which flattens
# the comparison the block exists to make. Subtracting the overhead measured in
# the size block leaves the marginal cost, which is what varies.
timing_overhead <- stats::setNames(timing_scaling$scaling$overhead_s,
                                   timing_scaling$scaling$arm)

k_complexity <- unique(dplyr::filter(timing_cells, block == "complexity")$k)
k_samples <- unique(dplyr::filter(timing_cells, block == "samples")$k)

stopifnot(length(k_complexity) == 1L, length(k_samples) == 1L)

timing_complexity <- timing_scaling$complexity |>
      dplyr::mutate(
            arm_ref = dplyr::if_else(scale == "M", "m", "beta"),
            marginal_ms = per_target_ms -
                  timing_overhead[arm_ref] * 1000 / k_complexity)

timing_samples <- timing_scaling$samples |>
      dplyr::mutate(marginal_ms = per_target_ms -
                          timing_overhead[arm] * 1000 / k_samples)

# The coherence check on that subtraction: rung 3 of the complexity ladder is
# the full-run model, so its marginal cost has to reproduce the slope the size
# block measured independently for the same arm.
timing_rung3 <- timing_complexity |>
      dplyr::filter(ladder == 3) |>
      dplyr::transmute(arm = arm_ref, ladder_ms = marginal_ms) |>
      dplyr::inner_join(dplyr::select(timing_tab, arm, per_target_ms),
                        by = "arm") |>
      dplyr::mutate(diff_pct = 100 * (ladder_ms - per_target_ms) / per_target_ms)

timing_anchor <- timing_scaling$anchor

# Display strings, precomputed so that the table captions carry no quoting of
# their own: a caption is a YAML scalar, and nesting escaped quotes inside one
# is a rendering failure waiting to happen.
full_k_fmt <- format(unique(full_timing$k), big.mark = " ")
full_n_samples <- unique(full_timing$n)
timing_k_max_fmt <- format(timing_k_max, big.mark = " ")
timing_k_full_fmt <- format(unique(timing_tab$k_full), big.mark = " ")
timing_extrap_fmt <- sprintf("%.0f", timing_extrap_factor)
k_complexity_fmt <- format(k_complexity, big.mark = " ")

```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-timing-full
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Elapsed wall-clock time of the full run, one `seqwrap()` call per arm, on `r timing_cores` cores. Each arm fitted the same `r full_k_fmt` positions in `r full_n_samples` samples."

full_timing |>
      dplyr::transmute(model = lab_model(model),
                       scale = dplyr::if_else(scale == "beta",
                                              "&beta;", "M"),
                       estimator,
                       hours,
                       per_target_ms = 1000 * elapsed / k) |>
      gt() |>
      fmt_number(columns = hours, decimals = 2) |>
      fmt_number(columns = per_target_ms, decimals = 1) |>
      gt::cols_label(model = "Model",
                     scale = "Scale",
                     estimator = "Estimator",
                     hours = "Hours",
                     per_target_ms = md("Per position<br>(ms)")) |>
      fmt_markdown(columns = c("model", "scale"))

```

The cost of a `seqwrap()` call is a fixed overhead plus a constant cost per target. Across the four arms the overhead is `r sprintf("%.0f", min(timing_tab$overhead_s))`--`r sprintf("%.0f", max(timing_tab$overhead_s))` seconds, essentially the same in every arm, which is what it should be if it is cluster start-up and data export rather than model fitting. The marginal cost per target is what separates the arms, and it separates them by estimator rather than by scale: REML costs `r sprintf("%.1f", timing_tab$per_target_ms[timing_tab$arm == "m_reml"] / timing_tab$per_target_ms[timing_tab$arm == "m"])` times ML on the M scale and `r sprintf("%.1f", timing_tab$per_target_ms[timing_tab$arm == "beta_reml"] / timing_tab$per_target_ms[timing_tab$arm == "beta"])` times on the &beta; scale (@tbl-timing-scaling). Part of that multiple is the Satterthwaite denominator df, which is computed on the REML arms only and requires a second differentiation of the likelihood; the rest is the REML fit itself.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-timing-scaling
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Cost of a `seqwrap()` call as a function of the number of targets, fitted on cells of at most `r timing_k_max_fmt` targets, and the resulting prediction of the full run. The exponent is $c$ in elapsed $= a + b k^{c}$, with linearity at $c = 1$; $p$ is for a quadratic term added to the linear fit. Predicted hours are for `r timing_k_full_fmt` targets, an extrapolation of `r timing_extrap_fmt`-fold beyond the largest cell measured."

timing_tab |>
      dplyr::mutate(model = lab_model(arm)) |>
      dplyr::select(model, estimator, overhead_s, per_target_ms, r2,
                    exponent, exponent_lo, exponent_hi, p_quadratic,
                    predicted_h, observed_h, error_pct) |>
      gt() |>
      fmt_number(columns = c(overhead_s, per_target_ms), decimals = 1) |>
      fmt_number(columns = c(r2, exponent, exponent_lo, exponent_hi),
                 decimals = 3) |>
      fmt_number(columns = p_quadratic, decimals = 3) |>
      fmt_number(columns = c(predicted_h, observed_h), decimals = 2) |>
      fmt_number(columns = error_pct, decimals = 1) |>
      gt::cols_merge(columns = c(exponent, exponent_lo, exponent_hi),
                     pattern = "{1} [{2}, {3}]") |>
      gt::cols_label(model = "Model",
                     estimator = "Estimator",
                     overhead_s = md("Overhead<br>(s)"),
                     per_target_ms = md("Per target<br>(ms)"),
                     r2 = md("Linear<br>*R*<sup>2</sup>"),
                     exponent = md("Exponent<br>[95% CI]"),
                     p_quadratic = md("*p*<br>quadratic"),
                     predicted_h = md("Predicted<br>hours"),
                     observed_h = md("Observed<br>hours"),
                     error_pct = md("Error<br>(%)")) |>
      fmt_markdown(columns = "model")

```

Two readings say that the cost is linear in the number of targets. The linear fit accounts for `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * min(timing_tab$r2))`% or more of the variance in every arm, and the exponent $c$ in elapsed $= a + b k^{c}$ is within sampling error of one in three of the four arms. It is not in `r lab_model("m_reml")`, where $c$ = `r sprintf("%.2f", timing_tab$exponent[timing_tab$arm == "m_reml"])` and a quadratic term is significant, so a slight super-linearity is detectable within the range measured. It does not persist: the chunk size `seqwrap()` chooses is itself a function of $k$ and the core count, so parallel granularity changes across the small-$k$ end of the size block in a way it does not change between there and the full run.

The check that decides whether any of this describes the full run is the extrapolation. Predicting from cells of at most `r format(timing_k_max, big.mark = " ")` targets to the `r format(unique(timing_tab$k_full), big.mark = " ")` the full run fitted is an extrapolation of `r sprintf("%.0f", timing_extrap_factor)`-fold, and nothing in the fit protects it. The predictions come out between `r sprintf("%.1f", min(timing_tab$error_pct))`% and `r sprintf("%+.1f", max(timing_tab$error_pct))`% of the observed times (@tbl-timing-scaling). A cost that grew faster than $k$ would not survive that, and neither would the `r sprintf("%.2f", timing_tab$exponent[timing_tab$arm == "m_reml"])` exponent if it were a property of the algorithm rather than of the range it was measured over.

What the marginal cost is made of can then be read from the two blocks that hold $k$ fixed and vary the model and the sample size instead (@tbl-timing-marginal). Both blocks report elapsed time divided by $k$, which still carries the per-call overhead amortised over the targets --- about `r sprintf("%.0f", 1000 * mean(timing_overhead) / k_complexity)` ms of it at $k$ = `r format(k_complexity, big.mark = " ")`, identically in every row --- so the overhead is subtracted before the rows are compared. The subtraction is checked against something it has to reproduce: rung 3 of the complexity ladder is the full run's own model, and its marginal cost agrees with the slope the size block measured independently for the same arm to within `r sprintf("%.0f", max(abs(timing_rung3$diff_pct)))`%.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-timing-marginal
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Marginal cost per target, with the per-call overhead removed, across the model ladder at $k$ = `r k_complexity_fmt`. `np` is the number of parameters the optimiser estimated. Rung 3 is the model the full run fitted."

timing_complexity |>
      dplyr::mutate(scale = dplyr::if_else(scale == "beta", "&beta;", "M")) |>
      dplyr::select(scale, ladder, model_label, np_opt, per_target_ms,
                    marginal_ms, converged) |>
      dplyr::arrange(scale, ladder) |>
      gt() |>
      fmt_number(columns = c(per_target_ms, marginal_ms), decimals = 1) |>
      fmt_number(columns = converged, decimals = 3) |>
      gt::cols_label(scale = "Scale",
                     ladder = "Rung",
                     model_label = "Model",
                     np_opt = "np",
                     per_target_ms = md("Elapsed / *k*<br>(ms)"),
                     marginal_ms = md("Marginal<br>(ms)"),
                     converged = "Converged") |>
      fmt_markdown(columns = "scale")

```

The ladder is where the cost actually lives. Going from a model with no random effect to the full run's `time + (1 | participant)` roughly triples the marginal cost on the M scale and quadruples it on the &beta; scale, and adding a second random effect adds `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * (timing_complexity$marginal_ms[timing_complexity$scale == "M" & timing_complexity$ladder == 5] / timing_complexity$marginal_ms[timing_complexity$scale == "M" & timing_complexity$ladder == 3] - 1))`% more on top of that. The number of arrays, by contrast, is close to free over the range available here: taking the participants from four to eight, and the arrays from `r min(timing_samples$n)` to `r max(timing_samples$n)`, moves the marginal cost by at most `r sprintf("%.0f", max(abs(100 * (dplyr::summarise(dplyr::group_by(timing_samples, arm), r = marginal_ms[which.max(n)] / marginal_ms[which.min(n)])$r - 1))))`% in any arm. The cost of a run of this kind is set by how many targets are fitted and how complicated the model is, not by how many samples each target has.

Finally, the anchor cell. It was re-run `r timing_anchor$n_anchor` times over the course of the experiment and measures the machine rather than the software: its mean elapsed time was `r sprintf("%.1f", timing_anchor$mean_s)` s with a coefficient of variation of `r sprintf("%.1f", timing_anchor$cv_pct)`%, and a regression on run order gives a slope of `r sprintf("%.2f", timing_anchor$slope_s_per_cell)` s per cell (*p* = `r sprintf("%.2f", timing_anchor$p_value)`). The machine did not drift, so cells run early and cells run late are comparable and the randomised run order did not have to absorb anything.

### Comparison with the published results

The supplementary tables of @seaborne2018 list the positions the original analysis called differentially methylated, one sheet per contrast against baseline, in `analysis/data/resource_data/seaborne2018-suppl.xlsx`. They are read here and compared with the four arms fitted above on the same deposited arrays.

The purpose of the comparison is not to audit the original study. It is to show what a calibrated per-position test returns on a real data set of this size, and how far that is from what an uncorrected threshold on a test that ignores the repeated-measures structure returns on the same arrays. The size of the two data sets is identical; only the procedure differs, and the permutation study above is what says which of the two procedures holds its nominal error rate.

```{r}
#| label: seaborne-supplement
#| eval: true

sup_file <- here::here("analysis/data/resource_data/seaborne2018-suppl.xlsx")

# Sheet 2A is a three-row summary; 2B--2D are the per-contrast lists. Only the
# first 13 columns carry data, the rest are the trailing empty columns Excel
# reports. The header sits on the second row of each sheet.
#
# `F(Error)` is 1 in every row: it is the numerator df of the test, not an F
# statistic, and is read as such below.
sup_sheets <- c(time3_loading   = "Supp 2B; Loading",
                time4_unloading = "Supp 2C; Unloading",
                time5_reloading = "Supp 2D; Reloading")

# The time level each sheet compares against baseline, and the sample counts
# actually deposited, which the degrees of freedom are checked against below.
sup_levels <- c(time3_loading = "3_loading", time4_unloading = "4_unloading",
                time5_reloading = "5_reloading")

meta_full <- readRDS(
      here::here("analysis/data/derived_data/seaborne-metadata.RDS"))

read_sup <- function(sheet) {
      x <- suppressMessages(
            readxl::read_excel(sup_file, sheet = sheet, skip = 1,
                               col_names = FALSE))[, 1:13]
      names(x) <- c("column", "id", "gene", "p_time", "p_pair", "meanratio",
                    "fc", "fc_desc", "estimate", "f_time", "ss_time",
                    "ss_error", "df_time")
      dplyr::mutate(x, dplyr::across(c(column, p_time, p_pair, meanratio, fc,
                                       estimate, f_time, ss_time, ss_error,
                                       df_time), as.numeric))
}

sup <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(sup_sheets, read_sup), .id = "term")

# The direction convention. `Estimate` is the baseline mean MINUS the
# condition mean on the beta scale: a POSITIVE estimate is a site that is
# hypomethylated relative to baseline at the later time point, which is how
# the FoldChange description column reads it ("Baseline up vs ..."). Our
# contrasts run the other way, condition minus baseline, so the two are
# compared through `-estimate` throughout.
stopifnot(
      all(grepl("^Baseline up", sup$fc_desc[sup$estimate > 0])),
      all(grepl("^Baseline down", sup$fc_desc[sup$estimate < 0])))

# The test behind the p-values. `p-value(Time)` and the pairwise p-value are
# the same number in every row, and both are reproduced by the F statistic on
# 1 and (n_baseline + n_condition - 2) denominator degrees of freedom: a
# two-group comparison in which the repeated measurements on a participant are
# treated as independent, not a repeated-measures analysis of the full design.
#
# The df is not assumed here, it is taken from the deposited sample counts and
# then checked against the reported p-values. That it agrees to rounding is
# also what establishes that the supplement was computed on the arrays we
# have: the same test on a different number of arrays would not reproduce.
stopifnot(identical(sup$p_time, sup$p_pair))

sup_ddf <- vapply(sup_levels, function(lv)
      sum(meta_full$time == "1_baseline") + sum(meta_full$time == lv) - 2,
      numeric(1))

sup_p_check <- sup |>
      dplyr::mutate(ddf = sup_ddf[term]) |>
      dplyr::summarise(.by = term,
                       ddf = dplyr::first(ddf),
                       max_dev = max(abs(pf(f_time, 1, ddf, lower.tail = FALSE) -
                                               p_pair)))

# The listed positions are everything below an uncorrected 0.05.
sup_alpha <- max(sup$p_pair)

sup_n <- sup |>
      dplyr::summarise(.by = term,
                       n_sup = dplyr::n(),
                       hyper = sum(estimate < 0),
                       hypo = sum(estimate > 0))

```

The p-values in the supplement are reproduced to `r sprintf("%.1e", max(sup_p_check$max_dev))`, the rounding of the file, by an F statistic on 1 and `r paste(sup_p_check$ddf, collapse = ", ")` denominator degrees of freedom for the three contrasts. Those are the degrees of freedom of a two-group comparison of the `r paste(sup_p_check$ddf + 2, collapse = ", ")` arrays deposited for each contrast, so the published lists come from a test that treats the repeated measurements on a participant as independent, computed on the same arrays that are refitted here. The threshold applied to them is an uncorrected p < `r sprintf("%.2f", sup_alpha)`.

#### Number of positions called

```{r}
#| label: tbl-seaborne-counts
#| eval: true
#| tbl-cap: "Positions called differentially methylated against baseline. The published column is the supplementary table of Seaborne et al., an uncorrected threshold on a two-group test; the remaining columns are the four arms fitted here on the same arrays, at the same uncorrected threshold and after Benjamini-Hochberg correction across all positions within a contrast. The Satterthwaite reference distribution is used where the arm provides one."

# Counts are formed with p.adjust() inside the summary rather than as a column
# on full_dat: the adjustment is over all positions within a contrast, and
# materialising it for 15.4 million rows is memory for nothing.
full_counts <- full_dat |>
      dplyr::filter(term %in% names(sup_sheets), convergence == 0) |>
      dplyr::mutate(p_use = dplyr::if_else(is.na(p_satt), p_wald, p_satt)) |>
      dplyr::summarise(.by = c(model, term),
                       n_tested = dplyr::n(),
                       p05 = sum(p_use < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
                       fdr05 = sum(p.adjust(p_use, "BH") < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE))

lab_contrast <- function(x) {
      dplyr::recode(as.character(x),
                    time3_loading   = "Loading",
                    time4_unloading = "Unloading",
                    time5_reloading = "Reloading")
}

full_counts |>
      dplyr::mutate(Contrast = lab_contrast(term)) |>
      dplyr::select(Contrast, model, p05, fdr05) |>
      tidyr::pivot_longer(c(p05, fdr05), names_to = "Threshold") |>
      tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = value) |>
      dplyr::left_join(sup_n |>
                             dplyr::mutate(Contrast = lab_contrast(term)) |>
                             dplyr::select(Contrast, Published = n_sup),
                       by = "Contrast") |>
      # The published lists exist at one threshold only, so the corrected row
      # is left empty rather than repeating the uncorrected count.
      dplyr::mutate(Published = dplyr::if_else(Threshold == "p05",
                                               Published, NA_integer_),
                    Threshold = dplyr::if_else(Threshold == "p05",
                                               "p < 0.05, uncorrected",
                                               "FDR < 0.05")) |>
      dplyr::relocate(Published, .after = Threshold) |>
      gt(groupname_col = "Contrast") |>
      gt::cols_label(beta = md("&beta;<sub>ML</sub>"),
                     beta_reml = md("&beta;<sub>REML</sub>"),
                     m = md("M<sub>ML</sub>"),
                     m_reml = md("M<sub>REML</sub>")) |>
      gt::tab_spanner(label = "This analysis",
                      columns = c(beta, beta_reml, m, m_reml)) |>
      fmt_number(columns = c(Published, beta, beta_reml, m, m_reml),
                 decimals = 0) |>
      sub_missing(missing_text = "--")

```

At the threshold the original analysis used, our arms return the same order of magnitude of positions as the published lists: tens of thousands per contrast out of `r format(n_full_sites, big.mark = " ")`. That is what an uncorrected 5% threshold returns whether or not anything is there. After correcting for the number of positions tested, the four arms return at most a few hundred positions, and the two arms the permutation study found to hold their nominal size -- REML with Satterthwaite denominator degrees of freedom -- return none at all.

#### Which positions

The counts are of a similar size; the positions are not the same ones.

```{r}
#| label: seaborne-overlap
#| eval: true

# Every position in the supplement, joined to our estimate of the same
# contrast at the same position.
sup_join <- full_dat |>
      dplyr::filter(term %in% names(sup_sheets), convergence == 0) |>
      dplyr::inner_join(dplyr::select(sup, id, term, sup_p = p_pair,
                                      sup_est = estimate),
                        by = c("target" = "id", "term"))

sup_cover <- sup |>
      dplyr::summarise(.by = term,
                       n_sup = dplyr::n(),
                       in_ours = sum(id %in% unique(full_dat$target)))

# Agreement, per arm and contrast:
#
# rep_005    the proportion of the published positions that this arm also puts
#            below 0.05 -- to be read against `base_005`, the proportion of ALL
#            positions this arm puts below 0.05. Equal values mean the
#            published list carries no information about our p-values.
# sign_agree the proportion on which the two analyses agree about the
#            direction of the change (their -estimate against ours).
# rho        Spearman correlation of the two p-value rankings.
sup_agree <- sup_join |>
      dplyr::mutate(p_use = dplyr::if_else(is.na(p_satt), p_wald, p_satt)) |>
      dplyr::summarise(.by = c(model, term),
                       n = dplyr::n(),
                       rep_005 = mean(p_use < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
                       sign_agree = mean(sign(estimate) == sign(-sup_est)),
                       rho = cor(-log10(p_use), -log10(sup_p),
                                 method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs"))

sup_base <- full_dat |>
      dplyr::filter(term %in% names(sup_sheets), convergence == 0) |>
      dplyr::mutate(p_use = dplyr::if_else(is.na(p_satt), p_wald, p_satt)) |>
      dplyr::summarise(.by = c(model, term),
                       base_005 = mean(p_use < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE))

sup_agree <- dplyr::left_join(sup_agree, sup_base, by = c("model", "term"))

```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-seaborne-overlap
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Agreement between the published lists and the fits reported here, per arm and contrast. Replicated is the proportion of the published positions that this arm also places below an uncorrected 0.05, and Background the proportion of all positions it places below 0.05; equality of the two means that knowing a position is on the published list says nothing about its p-value here. Direction is the proportion on which the two analyses agree about the sign of the change, and would be 0.5 for unrelated lists."

sup_agree |>
      dplyr::mutate(Contrast = lab_contrast(term), Model = lab_model(model)) |>
      dplyr::select(Contrast, Model, n, rep_005, base_005, sign_agree, rho) |>
      gt(groupname_col = "Contrast") |>
      gt::cols_label(n = "Positions", rep_005 = "Replicated",
                     base_005 = "Background", sign_agree = "Direction",
                     rho = md("Spearman &rho;")) |>
      fmt_number(columns = c(rep_005, base_005, sign_agree, rho),
                 decimals = 3) |>
      fmt_markdown(columns = "Model")

```

`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * mean(sup_cover$in_ours / sup_cover$n_sup))`% of the published positions survive the filtering applied here and can be compared at all. Of those, the proportion our fits also put below an uncorrected 0.05 is the proportion any arbitrary set of positions would reach, the two analyses agree about the direction of the change at close to the 50% expected of unrelated lists, and the rank correlation between the two sets of p-values is indistinguishable from zero (@tbl-seaborne-overlap).

This is not a disagreement between the two models. It survives fitting the published analysis itself:

```{r}
#| label: seaborne-rerun
#| eval: true

# Their test, re-run on the deposited arrays: a two-group comparison of
# baseline against the later time point on beta values, participants treated
# as independent, which is the test the 1 and 14 df identify. If the published
# statistics are recoverable from these arrays at all, this is what recovers
# them.
beta_vals <- minfi::getBeta(gset, offset = 100)
meta_full <- meta_full[match(colnames(beta_vals), meta_full$geo_accession), ]

two_group <- function(mat, i1, i2) {
      n1 <- length(i1); n2 <- length(i2)
      m1 <- rowMeans(mat[, i1, drop = FALSE])
      m2 <- rowMeans(mat[, i2, drop = FALSE])
      ss <- rowSums((mat[, i1, drop = FALSE] - m1)^2) +
            rowSums((mat[, i2, drop = FALSE] - m2)^2)
      df2 <- n1 + n2 - 2
      tstat <- (m1 - m2) / sqrt((ss / df2) * (1 / n1 + 1 / n2))
      data.frame(id = rownames(mat), rerun_est = m1 - m2, rerun_df = df2,
                 rerun_p = 2 * pt(-abs(tstat), df2))
}

i_base <- which(meta_full$time == "1_baseline")

rerun <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(names(sup_levels), function(tm)
      dplyr::mutate(two_group(beta_vals, i_base,
                              which(meta_full$time == sup_levels[[tm]])),
                    term = tm)))

rm(beta_vals)
gc()

# `rerun_est` is baseline minus condition, the same direction as their
# `estimate`, so these are directly comparable numbers rather than a
# transformation of ours.
sup_rerun <- sup |>
      dplyr::inner_join(rerun, by = c("id", "term")) |>
      dplyr::summarise(.by = term,
                       n = dplyr::n(),
                       rho_p = cor(rerun_p, p_pair, method = "spearman"),
                       r_est = cor(rerun_est, estimate),
                       sign_agree = mean(sign(rerun_est) == sign(estimate)),
                       med_reported = median(abs(estimate)),
                       med_observed = median(abs(rerun_est)))

```

Re-running the published test on the deposited arrays does not recover the published numbers either: the rank correlation between the re-run and the reported p-values is `r sprintf("%.3f", min(sup_rerun$rho_p))`--`r sprintf("%.3f", max(sup_rerun$rho_p))`, the two agree on the direction of the change for `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * min(sup_rerun$sign_agree))`--`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * max(sup_rerun$sign_agree))`% of the positions, and the reported effect sizes are about `r sprintf("%.0f", median(sup_rerun$med_reported / sup_rerun$med_observed))` times the mean differences those same positions actually show in the deposited data (median |&Delta;&beta;| of `r sprintf("%.3f", median(sup_rerun$med_reported))` reported against `r sprintf("%.3f", median(sup_rerun$med_observed))` observed). The identifiers themselves are valid EPIC positions and are paired with the same column numbers in all three sheets, so what cannot be reconciled is the pairing of the statistics with the positions rather than either one on its own. We therefore make no claim about which positions the original analysis would have called, and the comparison is confined to what does not depend on that pairing: the number of positions and the overall direction of change.

```{r}
#| label: fig-seaborne-overlap
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-cap: "Published p-values against the p-values obtained here for the same positions, M-values with REML and Satterthwaite denominator degrees of freedom. Each point is one position on one contrast. If the two analyses were measuring the same thing on the same arrays the points would concentrate along the diagonal."

sup_join |>
      dplyr::filter(model == "m_reml", !is.na(p_satt)) |>
      dplyr::mutate(Contrast = lab_contrast(term)) |>
      ggplot(aes(-log10(sup_p), -log10(p_satt))) +
      geom_point(alpha = 0.08, size = 0.5, colour = colors[3]) +
      geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, lty = 2, colour = "gray50") +
      facet_wrap(~ Contrast) +
      theme_classic() +
      labs(x = "Published &minus;log<sub>10</sub> p",
           y = "&minus;log<sub>10</sub> p, M<sub>REML</sub>") +
      theme(axis.title.x = ggtext::element_markdown(),
            axis.title.y = ggtext::element_markdown())

```

#### Direction of change

The conclusion drawn from the published lists is that hypomethylation predominates and is most pronounced after reloading, which is the evidence offered for a retained methylation signature. That claim is a property of the lists as a whole rather than of any one position, so it can be checked here even though the positions cannot be matched.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-seaborne-direction
#| eval: true
#| tbl-cap: "The proportion of positions that are hypomethylated relative to baseline: in the published lists, across all positions fitted here, and among the positions this analysis places below an uncorrected 0.05. A position is hypomethylated when the estimated change from baseline is negative."

dir_ours <- full_dat |>
      dplyr::filter(term %in% names(sup_sheets), convergence == 0) |>
      dplyr::mutate(p_use = dplyr::if_else(is.na(p_satt), p_wald, p_satt)) |>
      dplyr::summarise(.by = c(model, term),
                       all_hypo = mean(estimate < 0),
                       sig_hypo = mean(estimate[p_use < 0.05] < 0,
                                       na.rm = TRUE),
                       n_sig = sum(p_use < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE))

dir_ours |>
      dplyr::mutate(Contrast = lab_contrast(term), Model = lab_model(model)) |>
      dplyr::left_join(sup_n |>
                             dplyr::mutate(Contrast = lab_contrast(term),
                                           sup_hypo = hypo / n_sup) |>
                             dplyr::select(Contrast, sup_hypo),
                       by = "Contrast") |>
      dplyr::select(Contrast, Model, sup_hypo, all_hypo, sig_hypo) |>
      gt(groupname_col = "Contrast") |>
      gt::cols_label(sup_hypo = "Published", all_hypo = "All positions",
                     sig_hypo = md("p < 0.05")) |>
      gt::tab_spanner(label = "Proportion hypomethylated",
                      columns = c(sup_hypo, all_hypo, sig_hypo)) |>
      fmt_number(columns = c(sup_hypo, all_hypo, sig_hypo), decimals = 3) |>
      fmt_markdown(columns = "Model")

```

The ordering across the three contrasts is the opposite of the published one (@tbl-seaborne-direction). Here hypomethylation is most pronounced after loading and least pronounced after reloading, and the same ordering appears across all positions rather than only the called ones: the median change from baseline over the whole array is negative after loading and positive after reloading.

That ordering is, however, a property of the normalization rather than of the model. @seaborne2018 normalized with SWAN, a within-array method, where the pipeline used here (`analysis/R/methylation-case-study-dataprep.R`) uses functional normalization, which additionally removes between-array variation using the control probes. `analysis/R/methylation-normalization-check.R` repeats the filtering and the M<sub>REML</sub> fits on a subset under both, and the two disagree on exactly this point: under SWAN hypomethylation predominates at every time point and is most pronounced after reloading, the published ordering, and under functional normalization it is most pronounced after loading and reloading tips to net hypermethylation. The positions each returns differ correspondingly, with about half of an uncorrected 5% list specific to the normalization.

A direction shared by the majority of several hundred thousand positions, and reversible by a change of normalization, is a property of the arrays rather than of a set of positions, and neither ordering should be read as a methylation signature on its own. What does not depend on the normalization is the multiplicity: no position survives correction under either, in either the models fitted here or the test the original analysis used.
